name: Peter Burgoyne
heroAlt: Peter Burgoyne standing beside the sea in warm evening light
tributeHtml:
A life shaped by purpose, service and quiet determination.
Peter gave his time, skills and care generously.
shareDescription: A personal memorial song created from Peter’s story.
lyrics:
Born in February, in Derby town,
Peter learned to work and stand his ground.
From Chapel Street Market in his younger days,
He built his life in quiet, steadfast ways.

London became where his path would unfold,
With a curious mind and a spirit so bold.
Whatever the challenge, whatever was new,
He met it with purpose and always saw it through.

You made a life of purpose,
A life both strong and true.
You gave your time so freely
In everything you would do.

A husband, dad and grandad,
A loyal, trusted friend.
The lessons that you gave us
Will stay with us always.

At Burton’s dance hall, beneath the lights,
Peter met Diane on those London nights.
Caravan holidays, sea air and song,
Two people discovering where they belonged.

They married in June in the summer of ’70,
Then built their home and their family.
Karl, then Ross, then Louise came along,
And Peter stood beside them, dependable and strong.

He taught them to swim and be safe in the tide,
And watched their confidence grow by his side.
Then grandchildren came and brought joy to his days,
Each one dearly loved in their own special way.

Buster and Isla, Beau and Jolie,
Then Honey completed the family tree.
He watched every milestone with grandfather’s pride,
Content just to listen and stand by their side.

His lifeguard training opened a door,
To teach and to help and to give even more.
He worked with the swimmers, the young and disabled,
Sharing his knowledge whenever he was able.

He served on the Thames through the darkness and rain,
Keeping watch over London again and again.
At concerts and crossings, wherever the need,
He offered his time through his actions and deeds.

From Baxter Hoare to the Greenwich days,
Peter kept learning and finding new ways.
And when one door closed, he would start something new,
Finding another good job he could do.

From poolside to post room, friendships were made,
With stories and laughter that brightened each day.
Whatever the role and wherever he went,
He gave it his best and was quietly content.

He stacked up the wood for the cold winter days,
And worked in his boiler suit, dusty and grey.
The sound of the saw would ring out from the shed,
With plans for the next useful job in his head.

The neighbours would smile when a skip came in view,
For Peter could see what might still be of use.
Where others saw rubbish, he always saw more,
A purpose worth saving and bringing back home.

You made a life of purpose,
A life both full and true.
You gave your strength so freely
In everything you would do.

A husband, dad and grandad,
A loyal, trusted friend.
The love and time you gave us
Will never truly end.
rememberingParagraphs: Peter was hardworking, practical and endlessly curious. From his early days in Derby and London to the many roles he took on throughout his life, he met change with determination and was always ready to learn something new.

He was a devoted husband to Diane, a proud father to Karl, Ross and Louise, and a much-loved grandad to Buster, Isla, Beau, Jolie and Honey. His friendships, his love of music, his swimming and lifesaving work, and his years serving on the Thames all reflected the loyalty and generosity he brought to the people around him.

Peter had a gift for seeing usefulness where others might not, whether in a new skill, a practical job or a piece of wood rescued for winter. The time he gave, the lessons he shared and the steady way he stood beside those he loved remain part of the family life he helped to build.
closingLine: A life of purpose, remembered with love.
storyParagraphs: Peter Burgoyne was born on 14 February 1948 in Derby to Roy and Joyce. He grew up with his older brother, David, and later, after his mother remarried, the family expanded to include Elizabeth and Paul.

His early years were spent in Derby, where he attended Gerard Street Primary School, before moving to London and continuing his education at Sir Philip Magnus Secondary School. Peter learned the value of hard work from a young age. He took a weekend job at Chapel Street Market in Islington and later began his working life with an electrical wholesaler on Gray’s Inn Road. It was the beginning of a long and varied career marked by reliability, curiosity and a willingness to learn.

In the 1960s, Peter met Diane at a dance hall in Burton’s. Their relationship grew through shared evenings, music and caravan holidays on the Isle of Wight. They married on 13 June 1970 at St Mary’s Abchurch in London and soon moved to Barnehurst. In 1978, they settled in Horton Kirby, where they built their family home and shared many years of life together.

Friends became an important part of that story. Ted, Francis and Ed helped Peter and Diane with the practical work of preparing their home, and Peter never forgot their kindness. Friendship mattered deeply to him, and throughout his life he remained loyal to the people he met through work, volunteering and family life.

Peter and Diane welcomed three children: Karl in 1976, Ross in 1979 and Louise in 1982. Peter was a devoted father who believed in teaching by doing. After completing a swimming teaching course, he made sure his children were confident and safe in the water. He took pride in helping them learn, grow and find their own way.

Later, becoming a grandfather brought him enormous happiness. Buster, Isla, Beau, Jolie and Honey each held a special place in his life. Peter loved watching them grow, hearing about their milestones and simply being present. His affection was often shown quietly — through time, interest, stories and the dependable way he stood alongside those he loved.

Peter’s sense of service extended far beyond his family. He served for nine years as a special constable with the Metropolitan Police Thames Division, patrolling the river, supporting public safety and helping at major events. It was a role he was proud of, and it brought lasting friendships with Rod, Colin and Fred.

Swimming and lifesaving also became a major part of his life. After training with the Royal Life Saving Society, Peter volunteered with West Kent Lifeguards, Hastings Lifeguards and Bexley Beavers Disabled Swimming Club. Through this work he formed a close friendship with Chris Dearing. Peter gave his time freely, not for reward, but because helping others came naturally to him.

His working life continued to evolve. At Baxter Hoare, first in London Bridge and later in Erith, he built a friendship with Paul Marshall that lasted for more than thirty years. When redundancy brought that chapter to an end, Peter used his lifeguarding and technical skills to begin a new career at the University of Greenwich.

There, he became responsible for swimming-pool maintenance and trained as a pool plant technician, mastering the demanding work of managing chemical systems and keeping the pool operating safely. He loved the independence, responsibility and familiar faces that came with the role. When the pool later closed, Peter adapted once again, moving into the post room at Woolwich, where he enjoyed the social side of the job and formed a strong friendship with his colleague Andy.

Peter retired in 2013, although retirement never meant becoming idle. He remained practical, energetic and resourceful. He collected wood from skips and surrounding villages, seeing value where others saw waste. Back at home, he would cut and prepare it for winter in his garage, usually dressed in the boiler suit that became almost part of his identity.

Neighbours grew used to seeing Peter searching for something useful, planning his next job or finding a new purpose for something that had been discarded. It reflected the way he approached life: prepared, inventive and unwilling to waste what could still be of value.

Peter lived a life shaped by work, family, friendship, service and quiet determination. He kept learning, kept contributing and kept finding practical ways to help. The stories he leaves behind are filled with music, swimming, the Thames, family milestones, rescued wood, old friendships and a lifetime of making himself useful.
His was a life of purpose — built steadily, generously and with love.
